speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would invite Members to express their views or raise questions on both Motions during the debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will still move and take the Treasury Bills motion separately to ensure that the procedural requirements are dealt with.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: However, this proposal to have the substantive debate for both Motions taking place now, will allow the substantive arguments to be captured cogently in a single debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These securities are issued not for Government spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Specifically, the Singapore Government Securities (SGS) are issued to develop the domestic debt market and provide financial institutions with high quality liquid assets to meet regulatory requirements; the Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS) are non-tradable bonds issued primarily to meet the investment needs of the Central Provident Fund (CPF); and the Singapore Savings Bonds (SSB) are issued to provide individual investors with a long-term savings option.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Separately, the Local Treasury Bills Act (LTBA) authorises the issuance of Treasury Bills, to develop the domestic short-term debt market and to meet market demand for short-term rated Singapore Government debt securities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the increases in the respective borrowing limits do not improve the Government's fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both the GSA and the LTBA provide for limits on the amounts that can be borrowed through the issuance of Government Securities and Treasury Bills respectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the LTBA, the last increase for the issuance limit took place in 2007, when Parliament approved the increase of the Government's issuance limit from S$30 billion to $60 billion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is therefore a need to raise these limits, to cater to the growth in demand for Government Securities and Treasury Bills expected over the next five years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: About 74% of this increase is expected to be issued to the CPF as SSGS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In other words, we issue this to CPF as Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS) to meet its investment needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The coupon rates which the SSGS earn for the CPF Board match the interest rates that CPF members receive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We expect CPF balances to increase due to growth in the resident labour force and wages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, the resident labour force grew by an average of 1% per year from 2015 to 2020.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over the same period, nominal median gross monthly income from work of full-time employed residents grew by 2.8% per year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Upcoming CPF policy enhancements, like the higher CPF contribution rates for older workers will also increase CPF's investment needs in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is for the 74% The remaining 26% of the increase under the GSA will be for the issuance of SGS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is to support the continued development of a vibrant SGS market, that serves as an anchor for the growth of corporate debt market, and to meet the increased demand for high quality liquid assets from financial institutions in tandem with the growth of our financial markets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Like SGS, we have seen an increase in demand for Treasury Bills from investors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Issuing more Treasury Bills will help meet market demand for high quality short-term Singapore dollar denominated papers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to monitor the market demand for both Government Securities and Treasury Bills and will increase the rate of issuance to meet this demand, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government will also put in place a new short-term cash management tool, where Treasury Bills can be issued on an ad-hoc basis to meet temporary cashflow mismatches.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government strives to maintain a healthy level of Government Deposits with MAS and has a variety of cashflow sources like tax revenue and land sales to meet our liquidity needs for day-to-day operations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The introduction of this new tool is part of the Government's on-going efforts to expand our cash management toolkit and will provide more operational flexibility to raise cash quickly, should any short-term cashflow mismatches occur in future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Issuing ad-hoc short-term bills for cash management is not a new concept, as countries from around the world like Sweden have similar cash management bills programme to meet their governments' temporary cashflow mismatches.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Such temporary cashflow mismatches may occur from time to time as we seek to optimise the Government's treasury and liquidity management and minimise the excess cash holdings in the Government's balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Cashflow mismatches can occur when there are unanticipated delays in cash inflow, which may coincide with an earlier-than-expected cash outflow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When this occurs, we would address this by tapping on our liquidity buffers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is, therefore, important for the Government to have diversified sources of liquidity for better risk management, and the ability to issue ad-hoc Treasury Bills when needed would provide the Government with greater operational flexibility to manage our liquidity needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To distinguish this from the regular Treasury Bills, the ad-hoc Treasury Bills will be called "Cash Management Treasury Bills", or CMTB in short.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should emphasise that issuing CMTB will only expand our cash management toolkit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Again, it does not increase our fiscal budget available for spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The increases in the borrowing limits are for specific market development and operational needs purposes and not to cover the Government's fiscal shortfall.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Any increase in the Government borrowings under the GSA and LTBA will correspondingly increase the Government's cash and liabilities but will not increase the Government's fiscal budget for spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is to ensure that the government of the day operate on a balanced budget basis, funding its expenditures with revenues received during the term of Government, which would also include the Net Investment Returns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Why then does the Government need to issue Government Securities and Treasury Bills, other than the Special SGS and Saving Bonds?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As I can hear from the Second Minister for Finance, the primary purpose is to help develop the domestic debt capital markets where, among the necessary ingredients, is to have a domestic risk-free Singapore dollar bond yield curve so that the other institutional and corporate debt issuers can benchmark upon to price their cost of borrowings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a tradable and liquid bond market – both SGS and Treasury Bills – is also key to strengthening Singapore's position as a premier financial centre as it draws in institutional investors and other eco-system players into the Singapore markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It also enables banks and institutional players to use the Government Securities as collaterals to manage their balance sheets as well as facilitate the development and growth of repurchase agreements and derivative products.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding, it is also important to periodically review and restate our policy position on the purpose and the use of Government Securities – whether it still remains relevant in the evolving landscape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Why are debt issuances by Government Statutory Boards not covered under the overall borrowing limits in this Act?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, given the flushed liquidity situation and increasingly more investible dollars chasing for limited quality investments, would our investment agencies like GIC and Temasek be able to find investment opportunities with acceptable risk-return trade-offs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, given our challenging fiscal position in the years ahead and that the Government is contemplating using borrowings to fund very large and long-term infrastructure projects, would the Government be considering using a certain portion of the SGS to finance such projects?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I think it is important to ascertain that again.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My final question relates to the negative interest rates that we have seen around the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many developed economies and their government securities are currently experiencing interest rates in negative territory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that these two Motions constitute a fairly narrow exercise of the Government Securities Act and the Treasury Bills Act for the purposes of raising the debt ceiling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am also aware that this is a fairly routine procedure, which is for the purposes of funding CPF as well as for raising liquidity needs in response to the growth of Singapore's capital markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I just wish to add two thoughts: one is to request some clarifications over the underlying assumptions behind the amount requested and, second, I would like to query whether this is a good time to actually be borrowing more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, what were the projections for GDP growth numbers that were used to derive this increase in the debt ceiling?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Did this take into account the changed economic conditions relative to what has recently transpired?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am requesting this clarification because I believe that there is actually substantial uncertainty over the way that the economy will subsequently evolve over the next few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But if you would indulge me and allow me to take a further step and pose the question very much in the spirit of the Bill – is this a good time to borrow, and why?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have previously shared with this House that governments operate on very different budget constraints and time horizons from that of a typical household.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accordingly, it is misleading to think of government indebtedness in the same manner as liabilities accrued either by a private firm or a household.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, because governments operate essentially on an infinite time horizon and they possess the unique ability to finance their expenditures with money creation, the usual concerns faced by private actors over short-term illiquidity do not generally apply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is, therefore, not only sound economics but, in fact, a fiduciary responsibility for our Government to consider whether debt finance fiscal policy might actually offer a superior value proposition to either drawing down on reserves or strict adherence to a reserves replenishment schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As context, it is useful to consider the evolution of two key drivers of borrowing costs as the other Member has mentioned – the inflation rate and the interest rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In advanced economies, expectations of future inflation are very well anchored.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, there is very little indication that prices are likely to move sharply in the deflationary or inflationary direction, providing a substantial degree of certainty for the future macro-economic environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Interest rates have also remained very low worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This limits the room for traditional monetary policy to operate since further reductions are constrained by the zero lower bound.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the case can even be made, and has been made, for how incurring additional debt may counter-intuitively improve national welfare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How would we ensure that fiscal spending, then, is wise?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, we should be willing to spend now when the economy remains weak and can benefit the most from additional stimulus from Government expenditures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As the Minister has shared, the securities under this Act are not to be used to finance expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the question then, is – why not?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such expenditures typically offer the most bang for the buck – when the Government spends specifically on investment in public goods, such as new educational retraining programmes or infrastructural needs, as opposed to funding Government consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, when spending on replacing lost income was crucial in the early stages of the pandemic recession and remains important for vulnerable groups now, such as those in Tier-1 and Tier-2 sectors, there should also be a clear transition plan away from purely supporting consumption to an investment, especially, if I may suggest, in human capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this general fact has not escaped the Government, which has sought, among other efforts, to increase SkillsFuture re-skilling programmes or by remaining committed to plans for expanding the MRT lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I would emphasise here the importance that these programmes are themselves efficiently targeted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, there should be a clear understanding of the extent to which SkillsFuture trainees subsequently secure jobs in the new industries that they have been retrained for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As another example, infrastructural work on domestically oriented infrastructure projects, such as MRT lines, should take priority over those that enhance purely international connectivity, such as the new airport terminal.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond the current borrowing limits, I also urge the Government to expand its financial management tools while keeping tight fiscal discipline to achieve better financial efficiency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as the Minister has said, these borrowings are actually not spent but managed and re-invested by the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Government does not need the funds because it has been running Budget surpluses since 1968, except for a few years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The surpluses are attributed to profitable land sales, steady economic growth, high domestic savings through the CPF scheme and seigniorage from the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Minister has also said, the issuance of Government Securities is actually for the development of the local bond and money markets, and for providing a safe investment instrument for the CPF funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I note that in Budget 2019, the Government has announced that it would study the option of using Government debt as part of the financing mix for long-term infrastructure projects that the Government would be taking on directly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In line with that, I ask whether the Government will consider to institutionalise a new borrowing limit which may be called the Development and Contingency Limit (DC Limit) to give more flexibility in fiscal management and to take advantage of the historically low interest rates.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This DC Limit should be separate from the current borrowing limits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, debt, in itself, is good for instilling financial discipline.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a well-researched fact that cash-rich companies perform badly in terms of financial efficiency and the same arguably applies to the management of a country’s finances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Injecting debt into our public projects will improve financial efficiency and, more importantly, transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, to draw down $52 billion in a short period of time may mean that GIC needs to liquidate some of its investments at unfavourable prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, not tapping GIC may allow it to realise an investment return higher than our borrowing cost, which gives us additional financial benefits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Needless to say, before we deploy more debt, we should ensure that all the cash in the public sector are properly managed in the first place.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I noted that the Government has already put in place the Centralised Liquidity Management scheme in November 2009 to centrally manage the cash of all Statutory Boards and Ministries and the weighted average yield from the scheme for the year ended 31 March 2020 was 1.93% per annum.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, my next question is whether the Government will go one step further and soak up the “excess cash” of the Statutory Boards and deploy the cash to longer term investments to yield a higher return.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Excess cash is defined as cash over and above what is required to run the operations of the Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not currently included in our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask whether the Government will be tightening up the budgeting process a little more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government currently employs a block-budgeting process where the whole budget is allocated to the Ministries in blocks, with the quantum increasing every year in line with GDP growth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each Ministry then uses its discretion to re-allocate the “block” to its individual projects and uses.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A zero-based budgeting process should be adopted instead whereby each project is re-evaluated every year by MOF.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Projects which have outlived their usefulness should be closed or scaled down promptly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On-going projects after reaching maturity should reduce their spending gradually every year to reinforce the importance of achieving efficiency gains.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These practices are common in the private sector and can also be adopted in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to ask whether the Government will look at increasing taxes to further boost our financial standing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, for the global capital markets, we should not give the impression that the GST is the only source.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, the Government has taken many conscious decisions to do away with many taxes, especially those related to the progressive tax regime.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, when GST was introduced in 1994, the Government started to reduce personal income tax and corporate income tax from 30% to 20% by 2007.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government abolished estate duty in 2008 and, at the same time, took out tax on interest income, in addition to the absence of capital gains tax and other forms of wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are also no additional taxes on foreigners although they do not need to contribute to CPF or pay premiums to the MediShield and CareShield schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You know, there is a time and season for everything under the sun.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members have raised many issues that are outside the scope of these two Acts and the Motions that I have raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I will try, nevertheless, to address some of the points that are raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Assoc Prof Jamus Lim gave us an economics tutorial on the virtues of using debt financing, and Mr Leong Mun Wai also agreed with the merits of using debt financing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But that is not the scope of today's Motions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will have a full presentation on the Government's plans when we are ready and we can have a full debate on the extent to which debt financing is used, the limits for such borrowing and the scope of such borrowing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will do that in due course.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong asked about Statutory Boards having excess cash.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are very mindful of the cash that is in Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have put in place a framework to look at centralised management of liquidity across the whole-of-Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, from time to time, very regularly, we will discuss with the Statutory Boards if, indeed, they do not have specific plans for use of these reserves, we may very well and we have in the past swept back the reserves into the Government funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that has happened and we will continue to do that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The point that Mr Leong raised is a valid one.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is an area close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I started my career in the Civil Service as a Budget Officer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have a framework of block budgets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is to give certainty and assurance to Ministries for spending and for planning.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But from time to time, we go in and we review Ministries' projects, Ministries' spending and we take a zero-based approach to make sure that there is value for money in Government spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And when the Government were to put up proposals for increase in taxes, please, we would certainly hope that the opposition Members of this House would also support us in making these moves in order to strengthen our fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I assure you, each time we make such a proposal, we will want our taxation system to be progressive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is already a very progressive system, in fact.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have highlighted this many times in this House.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have said that for every tax dollar that a person pays, if he is lower income, he gets $4 in benefits, a ratio of one to four.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whereas, if you are higher income, for every tax dollar you pay, you get much less in benefits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even in the way we do GST, we have introduced elements of progressivity because we have a permanent GST Voucher which we give back to the lower income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the whole basis of our taxation system is designed to be fair, to be progressive, to enable us to move towards a fairer and more equal society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are in complete agreement in moving in that direction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, there were some questions raised about assumptions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked about the assumptions behind the increase of the debt ceilings and I think Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked the same question.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These debt ceilings for the Singapore Government Securities, SGS and Treasury Bills are raised periodically.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Members have highlighted, it is almost like a routine exercise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The reason why we do this every four or five years is twofold.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The purposes of raising the debt ceiling and to issue bonds, SGS or SSGS are twofold.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Number one, to develop the domestic bond market; and number two, to meet the investment needs of the CPF and the CPF members.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What are the assumptions behind CPF members' needs growing?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is linked to resident workforce growth, CPF contribution rates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are quite predictable and the needs are growing and therefore, we need to cater for it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I said, the significant part of the increase will be put for SSGS purposes, which means for the needs of CPF and CPF members.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second area is to develop the domestic bond market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Here, it is not so much about the overall economic condition, but it is about the demand for high-quality assets from financial institutions in tandem with the development of our financial markets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We get that assessment from MAS, they tell us that there is strong demand, continued demand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, even in this period, there is continued strong demand for high-quality safe assets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And SGS and Treasury Bills are safe assets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is the basis for raising the debt limits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Mr Liang asked, how about that debt issuances by the Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Statutory Boards are separate legal entities from the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: From time to time, when we need to increase, we come back to Parliament and we seek Parliament's endorsement for an increase in these limits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Liang asked about borrowing for infrastructure too.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think similarly, we will address that separately.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He asked also about whether there will be newer variations of issuance like green bonds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is something we will consider, quite separate from this exercise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, when we think about borrowing and using debt as fiscal policy for funding of major infrastructure projects, we will study if they are possibilities for different types of issuances like the issuance of green bonds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is something that we monitor very closely.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In Singapore, the context is different because MAS uses an exchange rate policy, so, it is not constrained by zero interest rate like other central banks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If that were to happen, yes, indeed, there will be impact on both borrowers and savers and we will study very carefully should such a contingency arise, what sort of mitigating measures we can put in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, for now, our baseline, or based on what we are looking at, I do not think we are entering a negative interest rate environment, but we do expect interest rates to remain low for a while, which as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said, gives rise to the motivation to think about borrowing for projects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And like I said, that is something we are studying carefully and we will come back to this house with a fuller presentation when we are ready and have a fuller debate on it.
